---
title: "Module 5 — Position and boxplot"
subtitle: "Data Description | Part II — Summarising one variable"
date-modified: 2026-10-18
---

**The business question.** "The Wandering Fork" has 120 days of daily
revenue data per franchise. The owner wants to know: what is a
"typical" day, how spread out are the days, and are there any
wildly atypical days? This module teaches you to locate specific
points within a distribution — the median, quartiles, and percentiles
— and to build the boxplot, the single most information-dense chart
in descriptive statistics. We start with two trucks small enough to
compute by hand, and only then write the formulas.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

- Explain in one sentence what the median, the quartiles, a percentile,
  the IQR and a boxplot tell you about a set of days.
- Compute the median, quartiles, and any percentile of raw or grouped
  data.
- Apply linear interpolation to find a quantile in grouped
  (class-based) continuous data.
- Build a boxplot from the five-number summary and detect outliers
  with the fence rule.
- Read $\text{rank}(Q_p) = p\,(n+1)$ and the fence formulas aloud as
  sentences, and write them in symbols from a description in words.
- Use the interactive demo below to see how changing the quartiles
  reshapes a boxplot.

## Theory

### Same median, different weeks

Two Wandering Fork trucks recorded their revenue over the same six
days. The numbers are a simplified extract chosen so that you can
compute everything by hand.

| Day | Truck A "Regular week" (€) | Truck B "Festival week" (€) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | 420 | 420 |
| 2 | 540 | 1,100 |
| 3 | 300 | 300 |
| 4 | 500 | 500 |
| 5 | 380 | 380 |
| 6 | 460 | 460 |

The two weeks differ on day 2 only. Is Truck B's €1,100 simply a very
good day, or so unusual that a boxplot should flag it? And what would
you say about the "typical" day of each truck? Look at the figure
before computing anything (start with step 1).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
miniA = [420, 540, 300, 500, 380, 460]
miniB = [420, 1100, 300, 500, 380, 460]

miniStats = xs => {
  const s = [...xs].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const n = s.length;
  const q = p => {
    const r = p * (n + 1), k = Math.floor(r), f = r - k;
    return f === 0 ? s[k - 1] : s[k - 1] + f * (s[k] - s[k - 1]);
  };
  const q1 = q(0.25), me = q(0.5), q3 = q(0.75);
  const iqr = q3 - q1, lo = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, hi = q3 + 1.5 * iqr;
  const inside = s.filter(v => v >= lo && v <= hi);
  return {s, n, q1, me, q3, iqr, lo, hi,
    wl: Math.min(q1, ...inside), wh: Math.max(q3, ...inside),
    out: s.filter(v => v < lo || v > hi)};
}

miniFmt = v => Math.round(v).toLocaleString("en-US")

viewof miniStep = {
  const labels = ["1 · Sorted days", "2 · Quartiles", "3 · Fences and box"];
  const form = html`<form class="ojs-step-picker">Show: ${labels.map((l, i) =>
    html`<label> <input type="radio" name="miniStep" value="${i + 1}"
      ${i === 0 ? "checked" : ""}> ${l} </label>`)}</form>`;
  form.value = 1;
  form.oninput = () => {
    form.value = +form.querySelector("input:checked").value;
  };
  return form;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = 660, H = 350, BLUE = "steelblue", ORANGE = "darkorange";
  const RED = "#d9534f";
  const x = v => 90 + (v - 200) * (W - 120) / 1000;
  const trucks = [["Truck A", miniStats(miniA), 90],
                  ["Truck B", miniStats(miniB), 220]];
  let g = "";
  trucks.forEach(([name, st, yc]) => {
    g += `<text x="10" y="${yc + 5}" fill="currentColor"
      font-weight="bold">${name}</text>`;
    g += `<line x1="${x(200)}" x2="${x(1200)}" y1="${yc}" y2="${yc}"
      stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.2"/>`;
    if (miniStep === 3) {
      g += `<line x1="${x(st.wl)}" x2="${x(st.q1)}" y1="${yc}" y2="${yc}"
        stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/>
        <line x1="${x(st.q3)}" x2="${x(st.wh)}" y1="${yc}" y2="${yc}"
        stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/>
        <rect x="${x(st.q1)}" y="${yc - 25}" width="${x(st.q3) - x(st.q1)}"
        height="50" fill="${BLUE}" fill-opacity="0.35" stroke="currentColor"/>
        <line x1="${x(st.me)}" x2="${x(st.me)}" y1="${yc - 25}"
        y2="${yc + 25}" stroke="${ORANGE}" stroke-width="3"/>`;
      [[st.lo, "lower fence"], [st.hi, "upper fence"]].forEach(([f, t]) => {
        if (f >= 200 && f <= 1200) {
          g += `<line x1="${x(f)}" x2="${x(f)}" y1="${yc - 40}"
            y2="${yc + 40}" stroke="${RED}" stroke-dasharray="5 3"/>
            <text x="${x(f)}" y="${yc - 46}" text-anchor="middle"
            fill="${RED}" font-size="11">${t} ${miniFmt(f)}</text>`;
        }
      });
    }
    if (miniStep === 2) {
      [[st.q1, "Q1", -34], [st.me, "Me", 48], [st.q3, "Q3", -34]]
        .forEach(([v, t, dy]) => {
          g += `<line x1="${x(v)}" x2="${x(v)}" y1="${yc - 28}"
            y2="${yc + 28}" stroke="${ORANGE}" stroke-width="2"/>
            <text x="${x(v)}" y="${yc + dy}" text-anchor="middle"
            fill="${ORANGE}" font-size="12">${t} = ${miniFmt(v)}</text>`;
        });
    }
    st.s.forEach((v, i) => {
      const isOut = miniStep === 3 && st.out.includes(v);
      g += `<circle cx="${x(v)}" cy="${yc}" r="6"
        fill="${isOut ? "none" : BLUE}" stroke="${isOut ? RED : BLUE}"
        stroke-width="2"/>`;
      if (miniStep === 1) {
        g += `<text x="${x(v)}" y="${yc - 14}" text-anchor="middle"
          fill="currentColor" font-size="11">${i + 1}</text>`;
      }
    });
  });
  for (let t = 200; t <= 1200; t += 100) {
    g += `<line x1="${x(t)}" x2="${x(t)}" y1="${H - 50}" y2="${H - 44}"
      stroke="currentColor"/>
      <text x="${x(t)}" y="${H - 28}" text-anchor="middle"
      fill="currentColor" font-size="12">€${t}</text>`;
  }
  g += `<line x1="${x(200)}" x2="${x(1200)}" y1="${H - 50}" y2="${H - 50}"
    stroke="currentColor"/>`;
  return html`<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" width="100%" role="img"
    aria-label="Daily revenue of Truck A and Truck B on a number line">
    ${g}</svg>`;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const line = (name, st) => miniStep === 1
    ? `${name}: sorted days ${st.s.map(miniFmt).join(", ")}; n = ${st.n}, so the middle is at position (n + 1)/2 = ${(st.n + 1) / 2}.`
    : miniStep === 2
    ? `${name}: ranks ${[0.25, 0.5, 0.75].map(p => p * (st.n + 1)).join(", ")} give Q1 = ${miniFmt(st.q1)}, Me = ${miniFmt(st.me)}, Q3 = ${miniFmt(st.q3)}.`
    : `${name}: IQR = ${miniFmt(st.iqr)}; fences ${miniFmt(st.lo)} and ${miniFmt(st.hi)}; outliers: ${st.out.length ? st.out.map(miniFmt).join(", ") : "none"}.`;
  return html`<p><em>${line("Truck A", miniStats(miniA))}<br>${line("Truck B", miniStats(miniB))}</em></p>`;
}
```

### Median

**Try it.** Sort Truck A's six days from smallest to largest, then find
the middle of the list.

1. At which position (or positions) of the sorted list is the middle?
2. What is the median of Truck A?
3. Now drop day 6 (460): the median of the remaining five days?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

1. Sorted: 300, 380, 420, 460, 500, 540. With $n = 6$ the middle lies
   between positions 3 and 4, that is at position $(6+1)/2 = 3.5$.
2. The average of the 3rd and 4th values: $(420+460)/2 = 440$.
3. Sorted: 300, 380, 420, 500, 540. With $n = 5$ the middle is position
   $(5+1)/2 = 3$, so the median is 420.

Truck B's median is also 440: its extra-large day 2 is simply the
largest value and does not move the middle.

</details>

**See it.** Step 1 of the figure sorts each truck's days and numbers
them; the median sits halfway between the dots ranked 3 and 4.

In plain words: sort the days, then take the one in the middle (or the
average of the two in the middle).

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — median
The **median** $Me$ is the value that splits an ordered series into
two equal halves: at least 50% of observations are $\leq Me$ and at
least 50% are $\geq Me$. For $n$ ordered values, if $n$ is odd the
median is the value at position $(n+1)/2$; if $n$ is even, it is the
average of the two values at positions $n/2$ and $n/2+1$.
:::

### Quartiles (exclusive method)

The median cuts the days in two halves. Quartiles cut them in four
quarters.

**Try it.** Use Truck A's sorted days (300, 380, 420, 460, 500, 540,
$n = 6$). For each quartile, compute its rank $p\,(n+1)$, say between
which two sorted values it falls, and interpolate.

| Quartile | $p$ | Rank $p\,(n+1)$ | Between values | Value (€) |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| $Q_1$ | 0.25 | ? | ? | ? |
| $Q_2 = Me$ | 0.5 | ? | ? | ? |
| $Q_3$ | 0.75 | ? | ? | ? |

Your turn: compute the three quartiles of Truck B. What do you notice?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

**Truck A**

| Quartile | $p$ | Rank $p\,(n+1)$ | Between values | Value (€) |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| $Q_1$ | 0.25 | 1.75 | 1st (300) and 2nd (380) | $300 + 0.75\times 80 = 360$ |
| $Q_2 = Me$ | 0.5 | 3.5 | 3rd (420) and 4th (460) | $420 + 0.5\times 40 = 440$ |
| $Q_3$ | 0.75 | 5.25 | 5th (500) and 6th (540) | $500 + 0.25\times 40 = 510$ |

**Truck B** (sorted: 300, 380, 420, 460, 500, 1,100): the ranks are the
same, so $Q_1 = 360$ and $Me = 440$ exactly as for Truck A, and
$Q_3 = 500 + 0.25\times(1100-500) = 650$.

The €560 jump of day 2 (540 → 1,100) moved the maximum a lot, but
$Q_1$ and the median did not move at all, and $Q_3$ moved by 140.

</details>

**See it.** Step 2 of the figure marks the three quartiles on each
truck's sorted days; the rank tells you where to read them.

In plain words: to find $Q_1$, compute $0.25 \times (n+1)$; if the
result is 7.75, take the value 75% of the way between the 7th and
8th smallest observations. This is exactly the position formula from
OpenStax §2.2, and it matches Excel's `QUARTILE.EXC`.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — quartiles (exclusive method)
The three **quartiles** $Q_1, Q_2 (=Me), Q_3$ split an ordered series
into four equal quarters. Following the exclusive convention used
throughout this course (Excel's `QUARTILE.EXC`), the position of
$Q_p$ ($p=0.25, 0.5, 0.75$) in the ordered data is
$$
\text{rank}(Q_p) = p\,(n+1),
$$
interpolating linearly between the two surrounding observations when
the rank is not a whole number.
:::

#### Notation decoder: quartiles (exclusive method)

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (Truck A) |
|---|---|---|
| $n$ | "n" | 6 days |
| $p$ | "p" | 0.25, 0.5 or 0.75 |
| $\text{rank}(Q_p)$ | "the rank of Q sub p" | 1.75, 3.5, 5.25 |
| $p\,(n+1)$ | "p times n plus 1" | $0.25 \times 7 = 1.75$ |
| $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$ | "Q one, Q two, Q three" | 360, 440, 510 € |
| $Q_2 (=Me)$ | "Q two, which is the median" | 440 € |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the quartile at fraction $p$ sits at
rank $p$ times $n+1$ in the sorted data; when the rank is not a whole
number, take the value that fraction of the way between the two
neighbouring observations."

### Interquartile range and outlier fences

**Try it.** For each truck, use the quartiles you just found.

| | $Q_1$ | $Q_3$ | $Q_3 - Q_1$ | $Q_1 - 1.5\,(Q_3-Q_1)$ | $Q_3 + 1.5\,(Q_3-Q_1)$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Truck A | 360 | 510 | ? | ? | ? |
| Truck B | 360 | 650 | ? | ? | ? |

Is any day of either truck outside its interval of fences?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

| | $Q_1$ | $Q_3$ | $Q_3 - Q_1$ | Lower fence | Upper fence |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Truck A | 360 | 510 | 150 | $360 - 225 = 135$ | $510 + 225 = 735$ |
| Truck B | 360 | 650 | 290 | $360 - 435 = -75$ | $650 + 435 = 1{,}085$ |

- Truck A: all days lie between 300 and 540, inside $[135, 735]$: no
  outlier.
- Truck B: day 2 (1,100) is above 1,085: **a high outlier**. The other
  five days are inside $[-75, 1085]$.

Note that the outlier itself pushed the upper fence up (735 → 1,085);
even so, it still sticks out.

</details>

**See it.** Step 3 of the figure draws the two fences as dashed lines:
Truck B's €1,100 lies beyond the upper fence, Truck A's days all lie
inside. (Truck B's lower fence, −75, is off the axis.)

In plain words: the IQR measures the spread of the central 50% of
the data. The fences extend 1.5 IQRs beyond the box — anything
further out is an outlier.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — interquartile range and outlier fences
$$
IQR = Q_3 - Q_1, \qquad
\text{lower fence} = Q_1 - 1.5\,IQR, \qquad
\text{upper fence} = Q_3 + 1.5\,IQR.
$$
Any observation outside $[\text{lower fence}, \text{upper fence}]$ is
flagged as a statistical **outlier** on the boxplot.
:::

#### Notation decoder: interquartile range and outlier fences

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example |
|---|---|---|
| $IQR$ | "inter-quartile range" | 150 € (A), 290 € (B) |
| $Q_3 - Q_1$ | "Q three minus Q one" | $510-360$ (A), $650-360$ (B) |
| $1.5\,IQR$ | "one and a half IQRs" | 225 € (A), 435 € (B) |
| lower fence | "the lower fence" | 135 € (A), −75 € (B) |
| upper fence | "the upper fence" | 735 € (A), 1,085 € (B) |
| $[\text{lower fence}, \text{upper fence}]$ | "the interval from lower fence to upper fence" | $[135, 735]$ (A), $[-75, 1085]$ (B) |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the IQR is the distance from the first
to the third quartile; the fences lie one and a half IQRs below $Q_1$
and above $Q_3$, and any value outside them is an outlier."

### Boxplot

**Try it.** Complete the five-number summary of each truck, then decide
which days are plotted as separate dots.

| | $\min$ | $Q_1$ | $Me$ | $Q_3$ | $\max$ | Outliers |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Truck A | ? | ? | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| Truck B | ? | ? | ? | ? | ? | ? |

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

| | $\min$ | $Q_1$ | $Me$ | $Q_3$ | $\max$ | Outliers |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Truck A | 300 | 360 | 440 | 510 | 540 | none |
| Truck B | 300 | 360 | 440 | 650 | 1,100 | 1,100 |

Truck A's whiskers reach its minimum (300) and maximum (540). Truck B's
box runs from 360 to 650 and its €1,100 day is drawn as an individual
dot. With only six days, the largest day inside the fences (500) is
already inside the box, so Truck B has no visible upper whisker; with
more days a whisker normally extends beyond the box.

</details>

**See it.** Step 3 of the figure is exactly this picture: a box from
$Q_1$ to $Q_3$, an orange line at the median, whiskers, and any
outlier as an open dot.

In plain words: a boxplot is the five-number summary drawn on a number
line — the box holds the central half of the days, and dots flag the
days that are too far away to belong to the pack.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — boxplot
A **boxplot** draws the five-number summary
($\min, Q_1, Me, Q_3, \max$, or the fences if there are outliers) as
a box (from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$, split by a line at $Me$) with whiskers
extending to the most extreme non-outlier values; outliers are marked
individually.
:::

### Percentiles

Quartiles are three special cut points. A **percentile** is the same
idea for any fraction $p$ of the days.

**Try it.** Truck C recorded four Saturdays: 320, 400, 480, 640 €
($n = 4$, so the rank is $p \times 5$).

1. Find the ranks of $P_{20}$, $P_{40}$, $P_{60}$ and $P_{80}$, and read
   their values.
2. Find $P_{30}$ and $P_{70}$ by interpolation.
3. What rank would $P_{90}$ have? What does it mean?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

1. Ranks 1, 2, 3, 4, so $P_{20}=320$, $P_{40}=400$, $P_{60}=480$,
   $P_{80}=640$.
2. $P_{30}$ has rank 1.5: $320 + 0.5\times 80 = 360$. $P_{70}$ has rank
   3.5: $480 + 0.5\times 160 = 560$.
3. Rank $0.9 \times 5 = 4.5$ — beyond the 4th (last) value. With four
   observations the exclusive method cannot place $P_{90}$ (Excel's
   `PERCENTILE.EXC` returns an error); the largest percentile it can
   give is $P_{80}$.

</details>

**See it.** Each percentile is a position on the sorted line; $P_{30}$
and $P_{70}$ fall between two values.

| Sorted value (€) | 320 | 400 | 480 | 640 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Rank | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| Percentile at this rank | $P_{20}$ | $P_{40}$ | $P_{60}$ | $P_{80}$ |

Between ranks 1 and 2 lies $P_{30}$ (360); between ranks 3 and 4 lies
$P_{70}$ (560).

In plain words: the $p$-th percentile is the value below which a
fraction $p$ of the days lie; to find it, go to rank $p\,(n+1)$ in
the sorted data, interpolating if the rank is not whole.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — percentiles (exclusive method)
For any percentile $P_p$ ($0 < p < 1$), the position in the ordered
data is $\text{rank}(P_p) = p\,(n+1)$, interpolating when the rank
is not an integer. In Excel: `=PERCENTILE.EXC(range, p)`.
:::

#### Notation decoder: percentiles (exclusive method)

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (Truck C) |
|---|---|---|
| $P_p$ | "the p-th percentile" | $P_{30} = 360$ € |
| $p$ | "p" | 0.3 for $P_{30}$ |
| $0 < p < 1$ | "p strictly between 0 and 1" | 0.9 is allowed, but its rank is out of range for $n=4$ |
| $\text{rank}(P_p)$ | "the rank of P sub p" | 1.5 for $P_{30}$ |
| $p\,(n+1)$ | "p times n plus 1" | $0.3 \times 5 = 1.5$ |
| $n$ | "n" | 4 Saturdays |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the percentile at fraction $p$ sits at
rank $p$ times $n+1$ in the sorted data, interpolating when that rank
is not a whole number."

### Grouped-data interpolation

Sometimes you only have a class table, not the raw days. Truck A's six
days, grouped in classes of width 100 (as in
[Module 3](module-03.qmd)), look like this:

| Class (€) | Count | Cumulative count |
|---|---:|---:|
| [300, 400[ | 2 | 2 |
| [400, 500[ | 2 | 4 |
| [500, 600[ | 2 | 6 |

**Try it.** For each of $Q_1$, $Me$ and $Q_3$, compute the target
cumulative position $p\cdot n$, find the class that contains it, and
interpolate linearly inside that class.

| | Target $p\cdot n$ | Class | $N_{\text{before}}$ | $n_{\text{class}}$ | Estimate (€) |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $Q_1$ | ? | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| $Me$ | ? | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| $Q_3$ | ? | ? | ? | ? | ? |

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

| | Target $p\cdot n$ | Class | $N_{\text{before}}$ | $n_{\text{class}}$ | Estimate (€) |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $Q_1$ | 1.5 | [300, 400[ | 0 | 2 | $300 + \frac{1.5-0}{2}\times100 = 375$ |
| $Me$ | 3 | [400, 500[ | 2 | 2 | $400 + \frac{3-2}{2}\times100 = 450$ |
| $Q_3$ | 4.5 | [500, 600[ | 4 | 2 | $500 + \frac{4.5-4}{2}\times100 = 525$ |

Compare with the raw-data values 360, 440 and 510: close, but not
identical. The class table has forgotten where the days sit inside each
class.

</details>

**See it.** On the cumulative-count column, the target position falls
between two cumulative counts; the estimate is the same fraction of the
way across that class's width.

In plain words: find which class contains the target position, then
interpolate proportionally across that class's width.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — quantile in grouped continuous data
For a continuous variable grouped into classes, we cannot read $Q_p$
directly from a list of raw values — we interpolate *within* the
class that contains the target cumulative frequency. If class
$[L, L+h[$ has lower cumulative count $N_{\text{before}}$ (from all
earlier classes) and count $n_{\text{class}}$ of its own, and we seek
the value at cumulative position $p\cdot n$, linear interpolation
across the class width $h$ gives
$$
Q_p = L + \frac{p\,n - N_{\text{before}}}{n_{\text{class}}}\; h.
$$
:::

#### Notation decoder: quantile in grouped continuous data

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (median of Truck A) |
|---|---|---|
| $Q_p$ | "Q sub p" | $Me$, so $p = 0.5$: estimate 450 € |
| $[L, L+h[$ | "the class from L up to, not including, L plus h" | [400, 500[ |
| $L$ | "L" | 400 € (lower bound of the class) |
| $h$ | "h" | 100 € (class width) |
| $p\cdot n$ | "p times n" | $0.5 \times 6 = 3$ |
| $N_{\text{before}}$ | "N before" | 2 days in earlier classes |
| $n_{\text{class}}$ | "n of the class" | 2 days in the class |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "start at the lower bound of the class
that contains the target position, and move across the class by the
fraction of its days still needed to reach the target, times the class
width."

## Worked example

Using "The Wandering Fork"'s `daily_revenue_eur` ($n=30$), verified
in `data-model.md`:

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---:|
| Minimum | 407.59 |
| $Q_1$ (exclusive) | 506.61 |
| $Q_2 = Me$ | 643.63 |
| $Q_3$ (exclusive) | 729.99 |
| Maximum | 886.56 |
| $IQR = Q_3-Q_1$ | 223.39 |
| Lower fence | 171.52 |
| Upper fence | 1065.07 |

**Step 1 — locate $Q_1$.** With $n=30$, rank$(Q_1) = 0.25\times 31 =
7.75$: interpolate 75% of the way between the 7th and 8th smallest
values of the ordered `daily_revenue_eur` series:
$500.02 + 0.75\times(508.80-500.02) = 506.605 \approx 506.61$.

**Step 2 — locate $Q_3$.** rank$(Q_3) = 0.75\times 31 = 23.25$:
interpolate between the 23rd and 24th smallest values:
$725.66 + 0.25\times(742.99-725.66) = 729.9925 \approx 729.99$.

**Step 3 — fences and outliers.** Keeping the unrounded quartiles,
$IQR = 729.9925-506.605 = 223.3875 \approx 223.39$;
lower fence $= 506.605 - 1.5(223.3875) \approx 171.52$; upper fence
$= 729.9925+1.5(223.3875) \approx 1065.07$. The observed minimum (407.59) and
maximum (886.56) both lie **inside** the fences — "The Wandering
Fork" has **zero outliers** in its daily revenue, itself a useful
finding: 30 days of trading, however variable, never produced a
wildly atypical day.

**Step 4 — draw the boxplot.** Box from 506.61 to 729.99, median line
at 643.63, whiskers extending to the true min (407.59) and max
(886.56) since neither is an outlier.

**Step 5 — grouped-data check.** Using the class table from Module 3
to estimate $Q_1$ (target cumulative position $0.25\times30=7.5$):
cumulative count reaches 6 after [400,500[ and 12 after [500,600[, so
$Q_1$ lies in [500,600[ with $N_{\text{before}}=6$,
$n_{\text{class}}=6$, $h=100$:
$$
Q_1 \approx 500 + \frac{7.5-6}{6}\times100 = 525.
$$
This is close to, but not identical to, the raw-data value of 506.61
— the difference is the same class-grouping approximation error
discussed in Module 4.

## Proof / derivation

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Derivation — locating a quantile in grouped continuous data (click to expand)
For a continuous variable grouped into classes, we cannot read $Q_p$
directly from a list of raw values — we interpolate *within* the
class that contains the target cumulative frequency. If class
$[L, L+h[$ has lower cumulative count $N_{\text{before}}$ (from all
earlier classes) and count $n_{\text{class}}$ of its own, and we seek
the value at cumulative position $p\cdot n$, linear interpolation
across the class width $h$ gives
$$
Q_p = L + \frac{p\,n - N_{\text{before}}}{n_{\text{class}}}\; h.
$$

**Sanity check with our class table** (Module 3): to locate the
median ($p=0.5$, target position $0.5\times30=15$) in
`daily_revenue_eur`'s classes, the cumulative count reaches 12 after
[500,600[ and 20 after [600,700[, so the median lies in [600,700[
with $N_{\text{before}}=12$, $n_{\text{class}}=8$, $h=100$:
$$
Me \approx 600 + \frac{15-12}{8}\times 100 = 637.5,
$$
close to (though not identical to, because this formula uses grouped
midpoint approximations while the true value uses the raw
30 observations) the raw-data median of $643.63$ computed above —
the small gap is exactly the information lost when data is grouped
into classes.
:::

## Visual intuition

The boxplot **is** the five-number summary drawn as a picture: the
box's *width* is the IQR (how spread out the central 50% of days
are), the line's *position inside the box* shows whether the median
sits closer to $Q_1$ or to $Q_3$ (a first hint of asymmetry,
formalised in Module 7), and the *whisker lengths* show how far the
more extreme (but non-outlier) days stretch beyond the box.

Step 3 of the two-truck figure shows it on six days: Truck A's box is
150 € wide, Truck B's is 290 € wide, and the festival day is an open
dot far to the right of everything else.

## Interactive demo — boxplot from quartiles

Drag each slider to set the five-number summary and watch the
boxplot redraw. Starting values are "The Wandering Fork"'s verified
statistics.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const start = [["vmin", "Minimum", 407.59], ["q1", "Q1", 506.61],
                 ["med", "Median", 643.63], ["q3", "Q3", 729.99],
                 ["vmax", "Maximum", 886.56]];
  const root = html`<div class="ojs-demo">
    <p>Move the sliders (kept in min ≤ Q1 ≤ median ≤ Q3 ≤ max order) to
      see the boxplot and IQR/fences update live.</p>
    <form>${start.map(([name, label, v]) => html`<div><label>${label}:
      <input type="range" name="${name}" min="300" max="900" step="0.01"
        value="${v}"> <output>${v.toFixed(2)}</output></label></div>`)}</form>
    <p class="ojs-demo-info"></p>
    <div class="ojs-demo-chart"></div>
  </div>`;
  const form = root.querySelector("form");

  function redraw() {
    const inputs = [...form.querySelectorAll("input")];
    inputs.forEach(el => {
      el.parentNode.querySelector("output").textContent = el.valueAsNumber.toFixed(2);
    });
    const [vmin, q1, med, q3, vmax] = inputs.map(el => el.valueAsNumber)
      .sort((a, b) => a - b);
    const iqr = q3 - q1, lo = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, hi = q3 + 1.5 * iqr;
    const outlier = vmin < lo || vmax > hi;
    root.querySelector(".ojs-demo-info").innerHTML =
      `IQR = ${iqr.toFixed(2)} · Lower fence = ${lo.toFixed(2)} ·
       Upper fence = ${hi.toFixed(2)}<br>${outlier
         ? "⚠️ min/max beyond fences — would be plotted as outliers"
         : "✅ no outliers"}`;

    const W = 660, Ht = 220, L = 30, R = 30;
    const x = v => L + (v - 300) * (W - L - R) / 600;
    const yc = 105, bh = 50;
    let g = `<text x="${W / 2}" y="18" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor"
      font-size="14">Boxplot from the five-number summary</text>`;
    for (let v = 300; v <= 900; v += 100) {
      g += `<line x1="${x(v)}" x2="${x(v)}" y1="40" y2="170"
        stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.15"/>
        <text x="${x(v)}" y="190" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor"
        font-size="11">${v}</text>`;
    }
    g += `<line x1="${x(vmin)}" x2="${x(q1)}" y1="${yc}" y2="${yc}"
        stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <line x1="${x(q3)}" x2="${x(vmax)}" y1="${yc}" y2="${yc}"
        stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <line x1="${x(vmin)}" x2="${x(vmin)}" y1="${yc - 15}" y2="${yc + 15}"
        stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <line x1="${x(vmax)}" x2="${x(vmax)}" y1="${yc - 15}" y2="${yc + 15}"
        stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <rect x="${x(q1)}" y="${yc - bh / 2}" width="${x(q3) - x(q1)}"
        height="${bh}" fill="steelblue" stroke="currentColor"/>
      <line x1="${x(med)}" x2="${x(med)}" y1="${yc - bh / 2}"
        y2="${yc + bh / 2}" stroke="darkorange" stroke-width="3"/>
      <text x="${W / 2}" y="212" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor"
        font-size="12">Value</text>`;
    root.querySelector(".ojs-demo-chart").innerHTML =
      `<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${Ht}" width="100%" role="img"
        aria-label="Boxplot from the five-number summary">${g}</svg>`;
  }
  form.addEventListener("input", redraw);
  redraw();
  return root;
}
```

## Exercises

All exercises below are done by hand; the Excel ones are in the
[homework](#homework-excel-lab).

::: {#exr-median-position name="Median position"}
For an ordered series of $n=24$ values, at which position(s) do you
read the median?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

$n=24$ is even, so the median is the average of the
values at positions $n/2=12$ and $n/2+1=13$.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-outlier-check name="Outlier check"}
A single unusually bad day of $\text{daily\_revenue\_eur} = 100$ is
added to "The Wandering Fork"'s data. Using the fences computed above
(171.52 / 1065.07, before recomputing the quartiles for the new
$n=31$ sample), would this new day be flagged as an outlier?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Yes: $100 < 171.52$ (the lower fence), so it would be
flagged as a low outlier — a day that badly underperformed relative
to the rest of the trading period.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-grouped-interpolation name="Grouped-data interpolation"}
Using the class table from Module 3, estimate $Q_1$ for
`daily_revenue_eur` (target cumulative position $0.25\times30=7.5$).

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Cumulative count reaches 6 after [400,500[ and 12 after
[500,600[, so $Q_1$ lies in [500,600[ with $N_{\text{before}}=6$,
$n_{\text{class}}=6$, $h=100$:
$$
Q_1 \approx 500 + \frac{7.5-6}{6}\times100 = 525.
$$
This is close to, but not identical to, the raw-data value of 506.61
— the difference is the same class-grouping approximation error
discussed in this module's proof.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-formula-words name="Formula to words"}
(a) Read $\text{rank}(Q_p) = p\,(n+1)$ aloud as one sentence. For
$n=9$ and $p=0.75$, which rank do you get?

(b) Read $Q_3 + 1.5\,IQR$ aloud. Which indicator is it? Compute it for
the values 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 ($n=5$: $Q_1 = 15$, $Q_3 = 45$).

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

(a) "The position of the quartile (or percentile) at fraction $p$ is
$p$ times $n+1$." For $n=9$: $0.75\times10 = 7.5$, halfway between the
7th and 8th values.

(b) "Go one and a half IQRs above the third quartile." It is the upper
fence. $IQR = 45-15 = 30$, so the upper fence is $45 + 1.5\times 30 =
90$.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-words-formula name="Words to formula"}
Write in symbols:

(a) "the gap between the third and the first quartile";
(b) "the rank of the 30th percentile among $n$ values";
(c) "a value $x$ is a high outlier";
(d) "the median of $n$ values when $n$ is odd".

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

(a) $IQR = Q_3 - Q_1$.
(b) $\text{rank}(P_{0.3}) = 0.3\,(n+1)$.
(c) $x > Q_3 + 1.5\,IQR$.
(d) The value at position $(n+1)/2$.

</details>
:::

## Common mistakes

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Watch out
- **Using `QUARTILE.INC` instead of `QUARTILE.EXC`.** The course
  standard is the exclusive method (position $(n+1)p$); mixing them
  gives inconsistent quartiles, especially on small samples.
- **Forgetting that percentiles need $0 < p < 1$ for `PERCENTILE.EXC`.**
  `p=0` or `p=1` will error — use `MIN`/`MAX` for the extremes.
- **Confusing the fence rule with standard deviations.** The 1.5×IQR
  rule is for boxplots; the "2 standard deviations" rule is for
  normal distributions — they are different tools.
- **Reading the median position as $n/2$ instead of $(n+1)/2$.** For
  odd $n$, $(n+1)/2$ gives the exact middle position; $n/2$ would be
  off by 0.5.
- **Using grouped-data interpolation when raw data is available.**
  The grouped formula is an approximation; prefer the raw-data
  quantile when you have the full dataset.
:::

## Exit check

Five minutes, no calculator needed except for question 4.

1. In one sentence, what does the IQR measure?
2. Why does one extreme day change the range a lot, but hardly move
   $Q_1$ and the median?
3. Read $\text{rank}(Q_p) = p\,(n+1)$ aloud as a sentence.
4. Compute $Q_1$, $Q_3$ and the $IQR$ (exclusive method) for the five
   values 10, 14, 18, 22, 50. Is 50 an outlier?
5. For $n=19$ ordered values, at which rank do you read $Q_1$?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The spread of the central 50% of the days: the distance between the
   first and the third quartile.
2. The range uses only the two most extreme values, so it follows an
   extreme day completely. The quartiles and the median depend on
   ranks in the middle of the sorted list, so a single day at the end
   barely changes them.
3. "The position of the quartile at fraction $p$ is $p$ times $n+1$ in
   the sorted data."
4. $n=5$: rank$(Q_1) = 1.5$, so $Q_1 = (10+14)/2 = 12$; rank$(Q_3) =
   4.5$, so $Q_3 = (22+50)/2 = 36$; $IQR = 24$. Upper fence
   $= 36 + 36 = 72$, so 50 is **not** an outlier.
5. $0.25\times(19+1) = 5$: exactly the 5th smallest value, no
   interpolation.

</details>

## Homework — Excel lab

Reproduce, in Excel, every indicator you computed by hand in class,
with `MEDIAN`, `QUARTILE.EXC`, `PERCENTILE.EXC`, `MIN` and `MAX`, then
apply them to the full dataset and build the boxplots.

**Estimated time:** about 50–60 minutes. Any spreadsheet application
works, at home or in a campus computer room.

**Follow-up:** a 10-minute debrief at the start of
[Module 6](module-06.qmd). Bring your Step 0 results and any question
on Homework 1–3.

### Using Excel

The sheet `harbour_30d` of `wandering-fork.xlsx` has the data. The
complete list of function names, with their French equivalents, is on
the [Excel functions](excel-functions.qmd) page.

| Concept | Excel function / steps |
|---|---|
| Median | `=MEDIAN(range)` |
| Quartiles (exclusive) | `=QUARTILE.EXC(range, 1)` / `(range, 2)` / `(range, 3)` |
| Arbitrary percentile | `=PERCENTILE.EXC(range, p)`, e.g. `p=0.9` for $P_{90}$ |
| IQR | `=QUARTILE.EXC(range,3)-QUARTILE.EXC(range,1)` |
| Boxplot | Select the data → **Insert → Statistical Chart → Box and Whisker** |

> **Why `QUARTILE.EXC`?** The course follows the $(n+1)\times p$
> position formula (OpenStax §2.2), which matches Excel's exclusive
> method. `QUARTILE.INC` (inclusive) gives different values on small
> samples — do not mix them.

For the **full table** (120 days per franchise) use the Excel Table
`tblFork` and add the franchise as one more condition, for example
`=QUARTILE.EXC(IF(tblFork[franchise]="Harbour",tblFork[daily_revenue_eur]),1)`
(entered as an array formula in older Excel, or use `FILTER` in
newer versions).

### Step 0 — check your class results

1. Type Truck A's six values (420, 540, 300, 500, 380, 460) in `A2:A7`,
   Truck B's (420, 1100, 300, 500, 380, 460) in `B2:B7` and Truck C's
   four Saturdays (320, 400, 480, 640) in `C2:C5`.
2. Below column A, compute `=MEDIAN(A2:A7)`, `=QUARTILE.EXC(A2:A7,1)`,
   `=QUARTILE.EXC(A2:A7,3)`, the IQR and the two fences (with
   `=Q1-1.5*IQR` and `=Q3+1.5*IQR` pointing to your cells). Repeat for
   column B.
3. For Truck C, compute `=PERCENTILE.EXC(C2:C5,0.3)`,
   `=PERCENTILE.EXC(C2:C5,0.7)` and `=PERCENTILE.EXC(C2:C5,0.9)`.
4. Compare every result with your hand computation.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Expected results</summary>

| Indicator | Truck A | Truck B |
|---|---:|---:|
| `MEDIAN` | 440 | 440 |
| `QUARTILE.EXC(…,1)` | 360 | 360 |
| `QUARTILE.EXC(…,3)` | 510 | 650 |
| IQR | 150 | 290 |
| Lower fence | 135 | −75 |
| Upper fence | 735 | 1,085 |

| Truck C | $P_{30}$ | $P_{70}$ | $P_{90}$ |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `PERCENTILE.EXC` | 360 | 560 | `#NUM!` |

`#NUM!` is expected for $P_{90}$: with $n=4$ its rank (4.5) is out of
range.

</details>

### Homework 1 (Excel) — Build the boxplot for Campus

In `wandering-fork.xlsx`, filter `franchise` to "Campus" and build a
boxplot for `daily_revenue_eur` (120 days). What are the five-number
summary and fences? Are there outliers?

**How to.** Filter `franchise` to "Campus", select the revenue column,
use **Insert → Statistical Chart → Box and Whisker**, and read the five
numbers with `MIN`, `QUARTILE.EXC` and `MAX`.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Campus 120-day: min = 23.85, Q1 = 236.07, median =
390.39, Q3 = 598.60, max = 1407.59. IQR = 362.54. Lower fence =
-307.74, upper fence = 1142.40. Three days exceed the upper fence
(1335.48, 1362.93 and 1407.59), so there are **three high outliers**
and no low one — consistent with Campus's right-skewed revenue
(skewness = 1.00).

</details>

### Homework 2 (Excel) — Percentile $P_{90}$ for Harbour revenue

Compute $P_{90}$ for Harbour's 120-day `daily_revenue_eur` using
`PERCENTILE.EXC`. What does this value mean?

**How to.** Wrap the revenue column in `FILTER` for "Harbour" inside
`PERCENTILE.EXC`, with `p=0.9`.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

A filter on the sheet does not change what
`PERCENTILE.EXC` sees, so restrict the range with `FILTER`:

```text
=PERCENTILE.EXC(FILTER(tblFork[daily_revenue_eur],
                       tblFork[franchise]="Harbour"), 0.9)
```

This gives approximately 699.63. It means 90% of Harbour trading days
earned €699.63 or less; only the top 10% of days exceeded this amount.

</details>

### Homework 3 (Excel) — Compare franchises with side-by-side boxplots

Create side-by-side boxplots for Harbour and Campus `daily_revenue_eur`
(120 days each). What visual differences do you see?

**How to.** Put the two franchises' revenues in two adjacent columns
and select both before inserting the **Box and Whisker** chart; compare
the boxes, medians and dots.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

The two medians are almost level (~391 vs ~390), but
Harbour's box is narrower (IQR ~299 vs ~363) and Harbour has a single
high outlier (€1,050.00, day 80, above its upper fence of 1016.45).
Campus's box is wider, with a long upper whisker and three high
outliers (€1,335.48 to €1,407.59) — visually confirming the right
skew and higher variability seen in the numbers.

</details>
